take: The API’s 1.786 million barrel crude build for the week ending 18 September, set against continued draws in US gasoline and distillate, is the key signal that crude is loosening whilst products stay tight, keeping crack spreads elevated and reinforcing the EIA’s read-through from crude, retail margins and taxes into pump prices. On the freight side, Rotterdam bunker sales down more than a quarter this year whilst Antwerp rises is a live test of RED III fragmentation, and with Fujian Guohang’s $372 million move into LR2 tankers and heavylift, the product tanker orderbook is quietly building just as Europe’s bunker demand map redraws. The positioning angle is the divergence itself: crude builds with product draws normally supports the back end of the curve, but record US production of 13.8 million b/d forecast for 2026 and Norway’s August rebound to 1.882 million b/d cap the upside, so watch whether the API build is confirmed or faded. The cross-market link to watch is gasoil versus bunker: with Rotterdam volumes down and Spain about to add a second data point, any RED III-driven shift in VLSFO demand will show up in the gasoil-bunker spread before it shows in flat prices. In the next 24 hours, Xi’s arrival in Washington on 24 September to discuss reviving the $6 billion-a-year US LNG trade, contingent on lifting the 15% Chinese tariff, is the headline risk, whilst Iran rhetoric and the proposed $5 billion Gulf reconstruction fund keep a geopolitical bid under crude.

items.title: Public companies produce most U.S. crude oil and natural gas
items.summary: Publicly traded companies represent a tiny share of the total number of companies producing crude oil and natural gas in the United States, but they make up a large share of U.S. production. In 2025, publicly traded companies accounted for just 2% of about 12,000 oil and natural gas producers but produced 68% of the crude oil and natural gas in the Lower 48 states.

items.title: What goes into diesel prices?
items.summary: The price of distillate fuel oil, often sold as diesel, is driven by the price of crude oil, retail margins, distribution costs, taxes, and crack spreads, the indicator we use for refining margins. Tight global supplies of distillate fuel oil and elevated crude oil prices have driven prices higher in recent months.
